# Adapter: HTTP / REST An HTTP interface is a method plus a path. Discover both from how this project declares routes; framework names below are search seeds, not defaults. ## Interface Discovery + A published schema (OpenAPI, JSON Schema, GraphQL SDL) is the first source when the project keeps one current; check it against the route code it describes. + Otherwise find the route declarations: controller annotations (Spring `@GetMapping`, ASP.NET `[HttpGet]`, NestJS `@Get`), router registrations (Express, Koa, Gin, chi), or decorators (FastAPI, Flask). + Full path is every prefix that applies plus the route's own path: gateway prefix, application context or mount path, router or class-level prefix, method-level path. + Verify module layout in the target project; do not assume a fixed package or directory. + Completion criterion: handler, HTTP method, full path, request model, and response model are located. ## Address And Response Wrapper + Base URL: read server port, context or mount path, gateway prefix, README, or deployment docs. + API line: write `METHOD {baseUrl}{prefix}{path}` or the project profile's equivalent. + Response wrapper and status codes: read the wrapper fields and the statuses the handler and its error handling actually produce. The wrapper goes in the conventions section; the response table expands the business payload. ## Parameter Positions HTTP request tables include a Position column: `path`, `query`, `header`, `cookie`, or `body`. Read the position from the binding the handler uses, such as a parameter annotation, a typed extractor, or the request property it reads. For a request body, follow object fields to their leaves and mark them `body`. ## Auth Read existing declarations only: method or class annotations, route guards, middleware, filters, interceptors, security configuration, and path-prefix rules. If auth cannot be established, mark it `unconfirmed` and name the missing source in the reply. ## Requiredness + Resolve requiredness per concrete route and active parameter binding, including optional parameter types and declared defaults; document the effective default. + A path variable in a matched route template is required. Where a framework lets one handler serve a route without the variable, document the routes separately. + Query and header parameters: read the binding's own rule and any validation that can still reject the bound value. + Body fields: inspect the validation that actually runs on this route, whether a schema library, validation annotations with their groups, a deserializer, or hand-written checks. A cascade into a nested object validates it when present; it does not make the object required. Record conditional constraints explicitly. + Distinguish an absent request body from an absent, null, or empty field. ## ID Type Use the wire type declared by the handler signature, schema, or DTO. # {Interface or Feature} API Documentation > Scope: {interfaces or business chain covered; N operations}. > Protocol: `{rpc|http}`. Updated: {date}. Remove the sections the scope does not need. --- ## Conventions Everything every call shares, written once from verified project conventions: + RPC: dispatch or gateway endpoint, request envelope, and response envelope. + HTTP: base URL, context path, response wrapper, and credential position. + Auth, pagination, failure handling, ID and time formats. + Examples in this document are illustrative; real IDs and values come from the caller's data. --- ## Operations | # | Interface | Operation identifier or route | Summary | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | [{name}](#{name}) | `{operation identifier}` / `{METHOD} {path}` | {summary} | When these interfaces replace older ones, add the old route beside each row. --- ## 1. {name} - {display name} + **API**: RPC -> `{operation identifier or service.method}` / HTTP -> `{METHOD} {full path}` + **Auth**: only when it differs from Conventions. + Caller-visible preconditions, ordering or idempotency, when the interface has them. **Request** ({RequestClass}) A few fields fit a list: `{field}` ({type}, required) — {meaning}. Use a table for more: | Field | Type | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | {field} | {type} | required / optional / conditional / unconfirmed | {meaning; value, length or format; the condition for conditional; what to send while unconfirmed} | | {obj}.{sub} | {Type} | optional | {state when requiredness applies only if the parent is present} | | {list}[] | [{TypeName}](#{typename}) | optional | {a shared type is referenced, not expanded} | For HTTP add a Position column (path / query / header / body). ```json { "field": "value" } ``` **Response** `data` ({ResponseClass}) No payload: one line, such as "`data` is null on success". A shared type: name it and link to Types. Otherwise: | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | data.field | {Type} | {meaning; presence and nullability when the caller must handle them} | Add a response example when the shape is not obvious from the table. **Errors**: only those specific to this interface; shared handling is in Conventions. | Error code / HTTP status | Message | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | {code} | {message} | {condition} | --- Repeat the interface section until the inventory is complete. ## Types One section per type that more than one interface uses. ### {TypeName} | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | {field} | {type} | {meaning} | ## Enums If enum values come from a lookup interface, point to that interface instead of hard-coding the values here. ## Differences From The Old Interface, If Replacing One | # | Difference | Old | New | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | {what the caller must change} | {old} | {new} | ## Integration Notes, If Needed Cross-interface rules the caller follows: call order, fallback behavior, parameter priority. Add an interaction diagram only when it clarifies the caller's contract; read [DERIVED-VIEWS.md](DERIVED-VIEWS.md) before drawing one. --- name: horos description: Generates API docs for backend interfaces across protocols (RPC e.g. SOFABoot/Dubbo, and HTTP/REST) and across projects. Use when the user wants to document a single interface, a whole requirement's backend API, or the API changes on a branch. --- # Horos — API Documentation API documentation is a caller contract with one reader: the developer, or their agent, who will call these interfaces from this document alone. Every line is something that reader acts on. Implementation details stay out. Use this protocol-neutral spine with the relevant **adapter** in `adapters/{RPC|HTTP}.md`. ## Commands ```bash /organon:horos [--rpc|--http] Interface /organon:horos [--rpc|--http] Interface method /organon:horos --feature /organon:horos --diff [baseBranch] /organon:horos --batch I1 I2 ``` These are Claude Code forms; Codex takes the same arguments after `$organon:horos`. A standalone install drops the `organon:` prefix. Detect an unspecified protocol from how the interface is declared: routes or an HTTP schema mean HTTP; an exported service interface or IDL means RPC. ## Workflow ### 1. Establish scope and project conventions Resolve the requested interfaces, feature or comparison snapshot. Read applicable requirements and design notes for scope, business terms and caller constraints. Use `docs/api-doc-profile.md`, or root `.api-doc-profile.md`, as a discovery index. Recheck conventions relevant to this task against current sources. Update stale facts in an existing profile; create `docs/api-doc-profile.md` when reusable project conventions warrant it. Its fields are protocol, base endpoint, operation identifier, RPC request envelope, response wrapper, auth, required-field rule, module layout, ID convention, output directory and model document. Keep unresolved values `unknown`. A project may have a **model document**: an API document its callers already accepted, named by the user or recorded in the profile. When one exists, match its section order, naming, file-name style and level of detail, so a caller who knows one document can read the next. ### 2. Build the interface inventory Cover the requested interface or method. For a feature or diff, include changed and deleted operations, reused operations the feature needs, and operations affected through shared DTOs, validators, serializers, wrappers, auth, schemas or dispatch rules. Include design-named operations and constants that constrain their caller contract. Classify items as added, modified, deleted or reused; record unresolved consumers as coverage gaps. A diff alone cannot find reused interfaces. Ask once, with the inventory, only for unresolved user-owned scope, contract or compatibility decisions needed to proceed. Read factual values from their sources; mark missing evidence and its impact. Use code-declared wire types where contract authority leaves them open. ### 3. Parse Each Interface From Code - Interface declaration: extract address or route and operation identifier from verified project conventions. - Implementation and validation: trace auth, required fields and other caller guarantees through the active call path. Each guarantee needs the boundaries that establish and preserve it; a declaration or helper alone establishes only its local behavior. - Request and response models: resolve generics, wire names, ignored fields, null handling, defaults, and active validation paths. Follow nested objects and list elements to their leaves. - Completion criterion: you can name the source of each fact; what the sources cannot settle is an unconfirmed item with its next check. Distinguish declared intent from enforced behavior when they disagree. ### 4. Write Markdown - If the profile specifies an output directory, use it. Otherwise, use a filesystem glob to find where the project's existing API documents live and write beside them. Use `docs/api/` as the final fallback. Do not use `git ls-files` for discovery because it misses untracked docs. - Fill the model document's shape, or `TEMPLATE.md` without one, by [Write for the caller](#write-for-the-caller). - File names follow the model document's style; without one, `{Interface}_API_Doc.md`, `{feature}_API_Doc.md`, or `API_Changes_{date}.md`. - Output language: write the generated API document in the language explicitly requested by the user; if none is explicit, match the user's prompt language. Use a project documentation convention only when the user is silent. Keep code identifiers, field names, operation keys, and literal enum values unchanged. ### 5. Self-Check - Every Markdown anchor target exists. - The inventory, the operation table and the interface sections name the same operations; the scope line states their count. - Every line passes [Write for the caller](#write-for-the-caller). - Include caller-visible preconditions, conditional requirements, ordering, idempotency, and errors when supported. Check examples against documented fields, wire types, and constraints. - Known defects are not written as the target contract. Mention at most a short note pointing to the issue or test. ### 6. Deliver Reply with the document path and what stays off the page: the contract authority and source revision inspected, each unconfirmed item with its next check, coverage gaps, and work the document implies for other roles. ## Write for the caller The caller reads the document to write calling code, often with nothing else open. These rules decide what goes on the page. - **The page carries the contract; the reply carries how you know it.** On the page a fact is stated plainly, or marked `unconfirmed` where the caller must not rely on it yet. - **Only the caller's work.** Server configuration, data setup and constraints on other teams' code are other roles' work. - **Say each thing once.** The conventions section holds what every call shares: endpoint, envelope, auth, pagination, failure handling, and the one note that examples are illustrative. A type that more than one interface uses is defined once in the types section and referenced by name. An interface section holds only what is specific to it. - **Decide requiredness.** Each request field is `required`, `optional`, or `conditional` with its condition. One the sources cannot settle is `unconfirmed`, with what the caller should send meanwhile. Distinguish missing, null and empty where the server treats them differently. Failure to find a constraint does not prove a field optional. - **Size the entry to the interface.** A request with a few fields is a short list; a response with no payload is one line; tables are for many fields. Use `field.sub`, `field[].sub` and `data.field` paths for nesting. - **One document per handoff.** A document the user will send on its own is complete on its own: conventions, types, enums and every interface in its scope. Divide by the caller's unit of work, such as a module or a client feature, when the user names one. - **Replacing an older interface.** When callers move from old interfaces to new ones, add the old-to-new mapping and one section listing what differs for the caller. Everything else is stated once as the current contract. ## Contract Rules **Target contract**: state the intended external contract. It has two sources, which you report in the reply: - **Contract authority**: the approved contract, design, or published schema that defines what the interface owes. If none applies, use the code revision designated as the contract, or `unknown`. - **Implementation evidence**: the source revision or snapshot actually inspected. The authority decides the promises, including any structure, wire name, or type it states. Implementation evidence supplies what the authority leaves open. If code contradicts the authority, document the authority's version and treat the difference as a known defect. If authority is `unknown`, document the implementation evidence as the contract. In that case, no difference is called a defect. What the sources cannot settle, including whether the code produces the response it intends, is `unconfirmed`. When existing callers keep calling an interface that changed (`--diff`, a modified or deleted operation), read [COMPATIBILITY.md](COMPATIBILITY.md) for field-level change marking and compatibility verdicts. Callers moving to new interfaces get the replacement mapping above instead. ## Large inventories Divide work only when scope warrants it and delegation is authorized. Keep contract authority, implementation snapshot, project conventions and output ownership consistent across parts.
